title: Annual research review: Infant development, autism, and ADHD--early pathways to emerging disorders.

subsections.subsection_title: Dimensional and Overlapping Conceptualizations of Neurodevelopmental Conditions
subsections.content:
Contemporary developmental psychopathology increasingly treats autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) not as wholly discrete entities, but as conditions defined by continuously distributed traits that vary across the population and blend with typical development. Dimensional models better capture subthreshold symptoms, heterogeneity within diagnoses, and developmental change than strict categorical approaches, while also aligning with evidence that symptom domains show graded impairment rather than clear natural boundaries ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

This perspective is especially important for early development, where emerging social-communication differences, attentional regulation problems, motor atypicalities, and sensory features often cut across later diagnostic categories. Empirical work indicates substantial phenotypic and etiological overlap between autistic and ADHD behaviours, including in community samples, suggesting partly shared liability rather than independent disorder-specific pathways ref [1], ref [5], ref [6]. Twin and family studies further support correlated dimensions of inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and autistic traits, with shared genetic influences helping to explain frequent co-occurrence ref [1], ref [7].

For infant research, an overlapping dimensional framework shifts emphasis from predicting a single diagnosis to characterizing developmental profiles across interacting domains of social attention, executive control, arousal regulation, and adaptive functioning. Such an approach is conceptually useful because early neurodevelopmental risk may manifest as broad alterations in behavioural organization before later differentiation into ASD, ADHD, or combined presentations; it also helps explain why early markers often show limited diagnostic specificity when considered in isolation ref [2], ref [4], ref [6], ref [8].

subsections.subsection_title: Early Risk Factors and Prodromal Indicators
subsections.content:
Early risk factors for ASD and ADHD are best understood probabilistically: they index altered developmental liability rather than disorder-specific causation. Prenatal and perinatal exposures appear to contribute to this liability, with maternal stress during pregnancy associated with higher levels of both ADHD and autistic traits in early childhood, consistent with a transdiagnostic view of early neurodevelopmental risk ref [3]. Likewise, infants requiring neonatal intensive care show elevated rates of later ASD-related outcomes, and early medical complications in this group may interact with broader vulnerabilities in self-regulation, sensory responsivity, and social engagement ref [4].

Prodromal indicators emerge within the first year but are often subtle and non-specific. Prospective work suggests that infants later showing ASD or developmental language delay can be identified before 12 months through atypical patterns of attention, social communication, and early motor-behavioral functioning, although predictive precision remains limited at the individual level ref [5]. For ADHD, early markers in infancy and toddlerhood include elevated activity level, poorer sustained attention, irritability, weak effortful control, and delays in regulatory development, again pointing to broad perturbations in emerging executive-attentional systems rather than a single pathognomonic sign ref [6].

Taken together, the evidence supports a developmental framework in which early risk factors and prodromal signs are overlapping, dynamic, and shaped by cumulative transactions between biology and environment. This overlap helps explain why early manifestations may cut across later diagnostic boundaries, and why longitudinal follow-up is essential for distinguishing transient variation from clinically significant developmental pathways ref [3], ref [5], ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Atypical Early Growth and Physical Development
subsections.content:
Atypical somatic growth has been investigated as one of the earliest observable correlates of neurodevelopmental liability, particularly in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Several studies report accelerated postnatal growth in a subset of children with ASD, including increases in weight, length, and especially head circumference during the first years of life, consistent with an early generalized overgrowth phenotype rather than isolated macrocephaly ref [7], ref [8], ref [9]. This pattern has been described in both autism and Asperger/high-functioning presentations, although findings vary across samples and ascertainment strategies ref [10]. At the same time, evidence that body length and head circumference at birth are only relatively altered underscores that apparent overgrowth may reflect deviations in developmental trajectory after birth rather than marked prenatal enlargement alone ref [11].

Importantly, these growth signals are heterogeneous and nonspecific. Pilot work suggests that abnormal growth may also occur in other childhood psychiatric conditions, arguing against a simple one-to-one mapping between overgrowth and ASD and instead pointing to shared developmental perturbations with variable phenotypic expression ref [7]. More broadly, the literature has shifted from treating physical growth anomalies as diagnostic markers toward viewing them as probabilistic indicators of altered biological timing that may co-occur with atypical brain development and emerging behavioral symptoms.

Comparable developmental approaches have also been applied to ADHD, where longitudinal evidence links trajectories of physical growth with later symptom dimensions, suggesting that early growth patterns may index broader neurodevelopmental dysregulation rather than disorder-specific pathology ref [12]. Thus, atypical early growth is best conceptualized as one component of a multidimensional risk architecture: informative when integrated with family history, early behavior, and neural measures, but insufficient in isolation for predicting ASD or ADHD outcomes ref [8], ref [9], ref [12].

subsections.subsection_title: Brain Development and Connectivity in ASD and ADHD
subsections.content:
A developmental perspective suggests that neural atypicalities in ASD and ADHD emerge early and are better understood as alterations in growth trajectories and network organization than as static lesions. In ASD, convergent neuroanatomical work has highlighted early brain overgrowth in at least a subset of children, with altered cortical and subcortical development appearing during infancy and toddlerhood rather than only after diagnosis ref [14], ref [17]. In parallel, ADHD has been linked to distributed alterations in brain structure and delayed maturation of association networks, consistent with models emphasizing atypical neurodevelopmental timing rather than focal deficit alone ref [13], ref [7].

Prospective infant studies have been especially important in ASD. Infants who later develop ASD show early brain enlargement and elevated extra-axial cerebrospinal fluid, suggesting that macroscale brain differences can precede the consolidation of behavioral symptoms ref [14]. Longitudinal diffusion imaging further indicates that white matter fiber tract development differs from 6 to 24 months in infants who later meet criteria for ASD, implying that atypical connectivity is present during the prodromal period ref [16]. These findings align with broader syntheses arguing that functional connectivity in autism is not uniformly hypo- or hyperconnected, but changes with age, brain system, and developmental stage ref [15].

In ADHD, network-level approaches likewise point to altered connectivity, particularly within frontostriatal and long-range white matter systems relevant to attention and executive control. Diffusion tractography and graph-theoretic analyses in drug-naive boys have shown abnormal structural connectivity networks, supporting the view that ADHD involves inefficient large-scale communication rather than isolated regional pathology ref [13]. Dimensional evidence also suggests continuity between subclinical ADHD traits and brain structure, as current ADHD symptoms in healthy adults have been associated with total brain volume variation ref [18]. Across both conditions, the emerging picture is one of early, dynamic, and partly overlapping perturbations in brain growth and connectivity, although their developmental timing and system-specific expression may differ ref [15], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Early Developmental Domains in Infant Risk Trajectories
subsections.subsection_title: Language and Early Communicative Development
subsections.content:
Language and early communication are among the most intensively studied infant domains in pathways to later autism, and they also show broader links to neurodevelopmental risk. Prospective sibling studies indicate that infants later diagnosed with autism often show subtle early reductions in communicative behaviors, including atypical vocal production, slower growth in gesture and word use, and weaknesses in social-communicative reciprocity before frank diagnostic symptoms are fully consolidated ref [20], ref [21]. Importantly, these early differences are often quantitative rather than categorically deviant, fitting a developmental-risk framework in which delays in prelinguistic communication may index emerging divergence rather than a disorder-specific marker.

A consistent theme is that early language development is embedded within social attention. Infant gaze behavior and affective engagement at 6 months predict later language outcomes in both typical and at-risk groups, suggesting that diminished orienting to socially informative signals may constrain opportunities for communicative learning ref [22]. Relatedly, difficulties in gaze following and gaze reading are associated with poorer word learning in children at risk for autism, reinforcing the idea that language delay may partly arise from disrupted access to joint-attentional information ref [23]. Findings linking volitional oculomotor control with language status in autism further support cross-domain coupling between attentional control and communicative development ref [24].

Language trajectories also intersect with broader sensorimotor development and are not unique to autism. Individual differences in motor skill are associated with later language level in toddlerhood, and atypical gestural performance is reported across autism, developmental coordination disorder, and ADHD-related presentations ref [19], ref [26]. Community pediatric assessments likewise suggest that early developmental concerns can foreshadow both later autism-spectrum and ADHD problems ref [10]. Taken together, the evidence favors a transactional account in which vocal, gestural, attentional, and motor processes jointly scaffold early communication, with disorder-specific outcomes emerging from partially shared developmental liabilities.

subsections.section_title: Early Developmental Domains in Infant Risk Trajectories
subsections.subsection_title: Social Attention and Early Interpersonal Signals
subsections.content:
Social attention and early interpersonal signaling are among the most intensively studied infant markers of later autism, because they index how infants orient to, engage with, and learn from social partners. Retrospective home-movie studies and prospective infant-sibling cohorts converge in showing that difficulties are often subtle in the first months, but become more apparent across the first year in reduced social smiling, atypical eye contact, diminished response to name, and weaker coordination of gaze, affect, and action during dyadic exchange ref [27], ref [29], ref [32]. These changes are developmentally important because early social orienting normally scaffolds later joint attention and communicative learning.

Work on the development of attention in infancy further suggests that social engagement depends on the integration of looking, posture, and action, rather than on gaze alone ref [28]. In this context, infants’ orientation to socially relevant stimuli predicts later joint attention skills, supporting the view that early biases toward faces, voices, and interactive partners help organize emerging interpersonal communication ref [33]. By the preschool period, children with autism show clear impairments in initiating and responding to joint attention, indicating continuity from early social-attentional differences to later social-communicative phenotype ref [31]. Studies of face processing similarly report reduced or contextually atypical attention to faces in autism, implying that early social perception may be less preferentially tuned to interpersonal cues ref [30], ref [34].

Although ADHD is also associated with attentional atypicalities, available evidence suggests a partially different profile: deficits are more prominent in sustained attention and regulation than in the specific social-orienting and joint-attentional disturbances that characterize autism ref [35]. For infant risk models, the key implication is that early interpersonal signals may offer particular specificity for autism-related pathways when considered alongside broader attentional and regulatory features, rather than in isolation.

subsections.section_title: Early Developmental Domains in Infant Risk Trajectories
subsections.subsection_title: Early Motor Development and Sensorimotor Atypicalities
subsections.content:
Motor development has emerged as one of the earliest domains in which atypicality can be detected in infants who later develop autism. Prospective studies of high-risk infants and retrospective analyses converge in showing delays or qualitative differences in postural control, head control, spontaneous movement, and broader sensorimotor organization within the first year of life [1], ref [38], ref [40], ref [43]. More generally, Prechtl’s assessment of general movements established that early spontaneous motor patterns provide a sensitive index of neurodevelopmental integrity, and this framework has informed efforts to identify prodromal motor signatures relevant to later autism-related outcomes [4].

Within autism-risk cohorts, specific findings include poorer posture development, persistent head lag, and atypical movement patterns, suggesting that early motor differences are not merely secondary correlates but may be integral to developmental divergence [1], ref [38], ref [40]. These disturbances may also shape infants’ opportunities for learning: locomotor advances such as crawling support new forms of exploration and memory flexibility in typical development [7], implying that delays in motor milestones could constrain access to social and cognitive experience. Consistent with this view, infants later diagnosed with ASD show atypical object exploration by 12 months, including less functionally varied engagement with objects, linking sensorimotor behavior to downstream developmental pathways [2].

Motor atypicalities are also developmentally consequential because they predict later communicative outcomes. In infant siblings of autistic children, early fine motor skill predicts later expressive language [10], and oral- and manual-motor abilities in infancy and toddlerhood relate to subsequent speech fluency in autism [6]. Such findings support a developmental-cascade account in which early disruptions in motor planning, posture, and exploration may contribute to later social-communication difficulties. They also underscore the value of incorporating detailed motor phenotyping into early surveillance, including in medically vulnerable populations such as NICU infants later classified with ASD [8].

subsections.section_title: Early Developmental Domains in Infant Risk Trajectories
subsections.subsection_title: Temperament, Regulation, and Emerging Behavioral Risk
subsections.content:
Temperamental style and early regulatory capacities are increasingly viewed as important components of infant risk trajectories, particularly for ADHD but also for broader neurodevelopmental liability. Prospective work highlights elevated activity level, irritability/negative emotionality, poor state regulation, and emerging difficulties in inhibitory or effortful control as among the earliest behavioral signals associated with later ADHD-related outcomes ref [6], ref [50], ref [52]. More generally, models of temperament distinguish reactive tendencies from regulatory control, with the latter becoming a critical developmental organizer of attention, emotion regulation, and behavioral adaptation across early childhood ref [46], ref [54].

Longitudinal studies suggest that early negative emotionality and weak attentional regulation prospectively predict poorer cognitive and behavioral function, while infant focused attention may index resilience or vulnerability depending on broader neurobiological and environmental context ref [47], ref [48]. In parallel, severe sleep problems in infancy have been associated with later ADHD diagnosis, consistent with the view that dysregulated arousal and sleep-wake organization may be early manifestations of atypical self-regulation rather than isolated symptoms ref [51]. Neurobiological accounts further propose that early brainstem and autonomic functioning may scaffold later regulation of affect and behavior, offering a potential mechanistic bridge between perinatal risk and emerging behavioral dysregulation ref [53].

At the same time, temperament markers are probabilistic and nonspecific. High activity in infancy does not uniformly predict later ADHD, underscoring the limited predictive value of single traits in isolation ref [45]. A multiple-pathway perspective is therefore useful: combinations of high reactive control problems, elevated emotionality, and low effortful control may identify infants on pathways toward ADHD, whereas overlapping profiles may also characterize children at risk for autism or other neurodevelopmental difficulties ref [49], ref [50]. The key challenge is to specify which patterns of early dysregulation persist, interact with environmental susceptibility, and differentiate later-emerging disorders.

subsections.section_title: Early Developmental Domains in Infant Risk Trajectories
subsections.subsection_title: Visual Attention and Orienting in Infancy
subsections.content:
Visual attention and orienting have emerged as candidate early markers linking infant neurodevelopment to later autism- and ADHD-related outcomes. Normative work shows rapid change across the first year in fixation, disengagement, and shifting efficiency, providing a developmental framework for interpreting risk-related deviations ref [63]. Within this framework, atypical orienting in infancy appears to index both domain-general attentional control and emerging social difficulties.

In infants at elevated likelihood for autism, several studies point to altered orienting and scanning from the first year onward. Prospective work has shown atypical response to name, suggesting reduced efficiency in orienting to socially salient auditory-visual cues ref [58]. Eye-tracking studies further indicate declining attention to eyes in infants later diagnosed with autism and atypical development of face-orienting mechanisms ref [15], ref [65]. At somewhat later ages, slowed habituation to faces and context-dependent differences in attention to social scenes suggest that atypical allocation of visual attention may affect how socially relevant information is sampled and updated over time ref [61], ref [62]. Structural correlates have also been reported, with atypical visual orienting at 7 months linked to white-matter microstructure in infants at risk for autism ref [64].

Attentional atypicalities may also foreshadow broader behavioral risk beyond autism-specific social phenotypes. Individual differences in infant fixation duration predict later attention and behavioral control, supporting continuity from early visual sampling styles to later self-regulation ref [59]. Similarly, movement-attention coupling in infancy has been associated with later attention problems in childhood ref [55]. Although much of the infant literature has focused on autism, later work in ADHD and autism suggests partially distinct downstream profiles, including visual-search alterations in ADHD and enhanced search performance in autism ref [56], ref [57]. Together, these findings support visual orienting as a transdiagnostically relevant early domain, while also indicating that the developmental meaning of early attentional atypicality depends on the broader cognitive and social context.

subsections.section_title: Interpretive and Etiological Issues in Emerging Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral Markers and Prodromal Presentations
subsections.content:
Research on emerging neurodevelopmental disorders has increasingly shifted from categorical onset models toward a prodromal perspective, in which early behavioral atypicalities are viewed as probabilistic indicators rather than disorder-specific signs. In autism, first-year markers are often subtle and include reduced social orienting, diminished eye contact, atypical affect sharing, and emerging differences in motor and attentional regulation, with many features becoming more evident over the second year of life rather than being uniformly present from birth ref [29], ref [3], ref [4]. This developmental unfolding is important because early abnormalities may reflect altered trajectories of social engagement and sensory-attentional processing rather than fixed symptom profiles.

A parallel issue arises in ADHD, where preschool precursors are typically expressed as broad difficulties in activity regulation, impulse control, sustained attention, and executive functioning rather than as the fully differentiated syndrome seen at school age. Early cognitive and behavioral indicators include elevated motor activity, delay aversion, poorer inhibitory control, and temperamental dysregulation, but these behaviors show limited specificity because they overlap with normative variation and with other developmental risks ref [52], ref [5], ref [6]. Accordingly, prodromal presentations in ADHD are best understood dimensionally, with severity, persistence, and cross-context impairment carrying more interpretive weight than any single behavior alone.

Across both autism and ADHD, the central interpretive challenge is that early markers are heterogeneous, developmentally dynamic, and frequently shared across disorders. Infant siblings and other high-risk cohorts show that combinations of social-communication atypicalities, attentional differences, and motor irregularities may precede later diagnosis, yet individual pathways remain highly variable ref [3], ref [4], ref [7]. Early behavioral markers therefore should be conceptualized as signals of altered neurodevelopmental liability embedded in transactional developmental processes, not as simple early equivalents of later diagnostic criteria ref [29], ref [52], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Interpretive and Etiological Issues in Emerging Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Predictive Assessment in Early Childhood
subsections.content:
Predictive assessment in early childhood is central to interpreting emerging neurodevelopmental disorders, but its value lies more in estimating probabilistic risk than in establishing stable early diagnosis. Community-based developmental surveillance can identify meaningful variation before formal diagnosis: early assessments by pediatric professionals have been shown to predict later autism spectrum and attention-deficit/hyperactivity problems, indicating that clinically observed concerns in routine practice carry incremental predictive information even outside specialist settings [1]. This is consistent with prospective infant-sibling work showing that deviations in social communication, attention, motor development, and regulatory behavior can precede categorical outcomes, although predictive strength varies by age and domain [2,3].

A major issue is that prediction improves when assessment is repeated over time and when multi-domain indicators are combined. Standardized instruments administered in the second year, including observational measures and parent report, show moderate utility for later autism outcomes, but accuracy is substantially lower in infancy because many features are not yet consolidated [4,5]. For ADHD-related outcomes, early markers are even less specific: elevated activity, poor effortful control, and attentional dysregulation in toddlerhood predict later symptoms at the population level, yet they also overlap with broader developmental and environmental risk [6,7]. Accordingly, models that integrate behavioral data with developmental history, family liability, and adaptive functioning are generally more informative than single-test approaches [3,8].

These findings have important interpretive implications. First, early assessment should be framed as dynamic risk stratification rather than binary case finding, especially in children with changing symptom profiles. Second, predictive tools must accommodate heterotypic continuity, whereby early regulatory or attentional problems may later differentiate into autism, ADHD, or mixed presentations. Finally, the usefulness of prediction depends on context: surveillance systems embedded in primary care may facilitate earlier support even when diagnostic precision is imperfect, shifting the goal from definitive early labeling to timely monitoring and intervention planning [1,7,8].

subsections.section_title: Interpretive and Etiological Issues in Emerging Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Comorbidity and Etiological Complexity in Neurodevelopmental Disorders
subsections.content:
A major interpretive challenge in infant risk research is that early neurodevelopmental liabilities rarely map neatly onto a single later diagnosis. Autism, ADHD, language disorder, anxiety, and intellectual impairment frequently co-occur, suggesting that early behavioral atypicalities may index shared developmental perturbations rather than disorder-specific prodromes. This concern is reinforced by population and family-genetic work showing substantial overlap in liability across neurodevelopmental syndromes and related psychopathology, with pleiotropic influences operating across traditional diagnostic boundaries [ref 2, ref 3, ref 4].

Syndromic and high-risk conditions illustrate this etiological complexity particularly clearly. In neurofibromatosis type 1, for example, population-based evidence indicates elevated rates of autism-related and other psychiatric difficulties, underscoring how a defined genetic condition can yield heterogeneous behavioral outcomes rather than a unitary phenotype [ref 1]. Comparable heterogeneity is seen in other genomic conditions associated with elevated autism and ADHD risk, where variable combinations of social-communicative, attentional, and cognitive impairments emerge over development [ref 5, ref 6]. Such findings argue against simple one-to-one models linking early markers to later categorical outcomes.

Accordingly, early assessment is best conceptualized within a transdiagnostic developmental framework. Dimensional approaches such as the ESSENCE model emphasize that early problems in attention, social communication, motor control, regulation, and learning often signal broad neurodevelopmental vulnerability requiring longitudinal follow-up rather than narrow disorder prediction [ref 7]. For infant studies, this means that apparent 'autism markers' may also foreshadow ADHD symptoms, cognitive difficulties, or mixed presentations, and that comorbidity should be treated as a central feature of developmental psychopathology rather than as a secondary complication [ref 3, ref 4, ref 7].

subsections.subsection_title: Early Intervention and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Work on infant siblings and other high-likelihood cohorts has shifted intervention thinking from remediation after diagnosis to support during the period when social communication, attention, and regulatory systems are still highly plastic. This translational perspective argues that infancy offers a window in which parent-mediated and developmentally embedded supports may alter cascading pathways to later autistic and ADHD-related difficulties, even when outcomes remain probabilistic rather than predetermined ref [67], ref [2], ref [3].

Clinically, the most promising approaches are those that target mechanisms already implicated in early risk: reciprocal engagement, sensory-regulatory adaptation, attentional control, and caregiver responsiveness. Trials in the first years of life suggest that coaching parents to follow the infant’s lead, scaffold interaction, and increase opportunities for contingent social learning can improve proximal social-communicative behaviors and parent-child interaction quality, with some evidence for effects on later symptom expression ref [4], ref [5], ref [6]. At the same time, infant intervention studies caution against expecting uniform prevention of categorical diagnoses; benefits may be better conceptualized as changes in developmental course, functional adaptation, and family well-being ref [67], ref [7].

For clinical translation, these findings support a stepped-care model in which repeated developmental surveillance is paired with low-risk, family-centered supports before diagnostic certainty is achieved. Such an approach is especially important because early markers often cut across autism and ADHD liabilities, implying that intervention should be transdiagnostic, individualized, and responsive to changing profiles rather than tied to a single disorder label ref [2], ref [3], ref [8].

subsections.subsection_title: Behavioral Markers for Assessment and Monitoring
subsections.content:
Behavioral markers are most clinically useful when they can be measured repeatedly, capture meaningful developmental change, and help distinguish broad neurodevelopmental liability from condition-specific pathways. In infancy and toddlerhood, candidate markers include atypical visual attention, reduced social orienting, differences in response to name, motor atypicalities, and altered patterns of habituation and disengagement. These measures are attractive for assessment and monitoring because they can often be obtained before reliable categorical diagnosis, and because they index processes—such as attention allocation and learning—that may mediate later social-communicative outcomes rather than merely reflect them [1, 2, 3].

Among these candidates, habituation-based paradigms are especially promising for longitudinal monitoring. Toddlers with elevated autism symptoms have been shown to exhibit slowed habituation to faces, suggesting reduced efficiency in encoding socially relevant information and a potential quantitative marker of emerging autistic traits [1]. This finding converges with prospective infant-sibling studies showing atypical attention disengagement and visual orienting in infants later diagnosed with autism, as well as altered trajectories of social attention across the first years of life [2, 4, 5]. Importantly, such markers should not be treated as disorder-specific in isolation: many reflect domain-general regulatory and attentional mechanisms that may also be implicated in ADHD risk, highlighting the need to interpret them developmentally and in multivariate combinations [3, 6].

For clinical translation, the strongest approach is likely to combine brief observational measures with repeated parent report and, where feasible, eye-tracking or structured laboratory tasks. Behavioral markers are unlikely to function as stand-alone screening tools, but they can improve monitoring of change, stratify risk, and inform treatment targets when embedded in developmental surveillance frameworks [4, 6, 7]. Methodologically, this requires attention to test-retest reliability, age sensitivity, and the distinction between markers of current state and predictors of later outcome. In practice, scalable marker batteries that track social attention, learning efficiency, and regulatory control may prove more useful than any single index for monitoring emerging autism-ADHD pathways over time [1, 3, 7].

subsections.subsection_title: Caregiving Contexts and Developmental Support
subsections.content:
Caregiving context is a key moderator of early developmental trajectories relevant to autism and ADHD, because infant neurocognitive vulnerabilities unfold within patterns of parental regulation, scaffolding, and stress exposure. Work linking maternal executive function to later child executive function suggests that caregiver capacities can shape the quality and consistency of support available for emerging self-regulation, above and beyond child characteristics alone ref [68]. This is especially pertinent in high-risk cohorts, where subtle early differences in attention control, arousal regulation, and social engagement may alter caregiver–infant transactions over time.

A transactional view is therefore clinically useful. Sensitive, contingent, and well-scaffolded caregiving supports attentional control, language, and emotion regulation, whereas elevated parenting stress and reduced synchrony may amplify difficulties in infants already showing atypical attentional or social profiles ref [2], ref [3]. In autism, parent-mediated approaches have shown that modifying the interactional environment can improve social communication and adaptive engagement in the first years of life ref [4], ref [5]. Parallel evidence from ADHD-relevant developmental pathways indicates that harsh or inconsistent parenting is associated with poorer regulation and greater externalizing risk, while warm, structured caregiving can buffer vulnerability ref [6], ref [7].

Methodologically, caregiving should not be treated merely as background context, but as a dynamic exposure to be measured repeatedly alongside infant behavior. Assessments that integrate parent mental health, executive function, responsivity, and family stress are likely to yield more accurate developmental forecasts and more individualized intervention targets ref [68], ref [3], ref [8]. Clinically, this argues for developmental support models that combine infant-focused monitoring with caregiver coaching, stress reduction, and adaptation of daily routines, rather than relying on child-centered symptom surveillance alone ref [4], ref [9].

subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostic Frameworks and Conceptual Models
subsections.content:
Diagnostic frameworks for infant pathways to autism and ADHD are increasingly shaped by the tension between categorical diagnosis and dimensional characterization. Developmental data suggest that early traits are broadly distributed, partially continuous with later symptom dimensions, and only gradually consolidate into recognizable clinical syndromes, arguing against a purely categorical view of emerging disorders ref [2]. In infancy, this is especially important because many early differences in attention, regulation, motor control, and social engagement are neither specific nor stable enough to map cleanly onto later DSM-defined outcomes.

A dimensional-developmental approach is therefore often more informative for early risk formulation than syndrome prediction alone. Models such as the Research Domain Criteria emphasize cross-cutting processes, while developmental psychopathology frameworks highlight equifinality, multifinality, and cascading effects across biological and caregiving systems ref [2], ref [3]. Consistent with this perspective, longitudinal infant-sibling and population studies indicate substantial overlap in early liabilities across autism and ADHD, including shared variation in executive attention, temperament, sensory responsivity, and activity level, alongside later divergence in symptom configuration ref [4], ref [5], ref [6].

Clinically, these conceptual shifts support transdiagnostic surveillance models that track functional dimensions over time rather than waiting for threshold-level disorder to emerge. At the same time, categories remain pragmatically important for service access, prognostic communication, and treatment planning ref [2]. The most useful framework may therefore be hybrid: categorical diagnoses retained for clinical decision-making, embedded within dimensional and developmental formulations that capture heterogeneity, comorbidity, and change across infancy and early childhood ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.subsection_title: Early Developmental Markers and Risk Trajectories
subsections.content:
Prospective infant-sibling and familial-risk designs indicate that early developmental markers of autism and ADHD are best understood as probabilistic deviations in developmental trajectories rather than disorder-specific signs present at birth. In infants later showing autism-related outcomes, atypicalities have been reported in social orienting and attentional engagement during the first year, including altered face orienting mechanisms and reduced attention to socially informative cues, although these effects are often subtle and unstable early in life ref [64], ref [43], ref [4]. Parallel work on ADHD risk highlights early variations in activity level, regulatory difficulties, and emerging attentional control, suggesting that vulnerabilities in arousal and executive-attentional systems may also be detectable before the preschool period ref [6], ref [5].

A central synthesis across studies is that early markers rarely map one-to-one onto later categorical outcomes. Instead, broad liabilities appear to unfold through cascading interactions among attention, social communication, motor development, and temperament. Prospective studies of infants later diagnosed with autism show developmental divergence over the first 2 years, with some infants appearing relatively typical in early infancy before displaying slowing or regression in social-communicative growth ref [43], ref [6]. For ADHD, early markers are similarly heterogeneous, with infant regulatory and attentional differences predicting later symptoms at the group level but offering limited individual-level specificity ref [6], ref [7].

These findings support a developmental-risk framework in which early behavioral markers index shared and partially overlapping neurodevelopmental liabilities. The key task is therefore not simply to identify the earliest sign, but to characterize risk trajectories, their timing, and the conditions under which early differences consolidate into autism, ADHD, co-occurring presentations, or broader atypical developmental profiles ref [4], ref [5], ref [7].

subsections.subsection_title: Attention, Motor, and Language Precursors
subsections.content:
Attention, motor, and language functions provide some of the earliest measurable clues to later neurodevelopmental divergence, although their predictive value is probabilistic rather than deterministic. In ADHD, preschool antecedents include elevated activity, poorer inhibitory control, delay aversion, and weaknesses in sustained or focused attention, suggesting that attentional regulation difficulties can be detected before formal diagnosis is possible ref [52]. Converging evidence from preterm cohorts likewise shows that early focused attention predicts later cognitive and behavioral outcome, underscoring attention as a broadly informative developmental signal rather than a disorder-specific marker ref [47].

Motor development also appears tightly linked to emerging social-communicative phenotypes. In infants at familial risk for autism, fine motor skill has been shown to predict later expressive language, consistent with the view that early motor competence may scaffold opportunities for exploration, joint engagement, and communicative practice ref [44]. More generally, atypical motor patterns in infancy and toddlerhood have been repeatedly associated with later autism-related outcomes, including delays in gesture, coordination, and broader adaptive functioning ref [4], ref [5]. These findings support models in which motor differences are not merely co-occurring features, but part of a cascading developmental process.

Language precursors cut across diagnostic boundaries. Early delays in expressive vocabulary, gesture use, and communicative reciprocity are common in children who later meet criteria for autism, but milder early language weaknesses can also accompany trajectories toward ADHD, particularly when attentional control constrains learning from the environment ref [52], ref [6]. The broader implication is that attention, motor skill, and language should be understood as interdependent developmental systems: disruptions in one domain may amplify risk in another, producing heterogeneous but partially overlapping pathways to later autism- and ADHD-related phenotypes ref [44], ref [7].

subsections.subsection_title: Overlap, Growth Patterns, and Cross-Disorder Phenotypes
subsections.content:
A consistent theme in prospective work is that early neurodevelopmental liabilities are not cleanly partitioned by diagnostic boundaries. Autistic traits and ADHD symptoms show substantial co-occurrence in population and familial designs, with twin data indicating partly shared genetic and developmental influences rather than entirely independent pathways ref [69]. This overlap is also evident phenotypically: infants later meeting criteria for one condition may show attentional atypicalities, regulatory difficulties, or social-communication variation that are not specific to a single disorder, supporting a dimensional view of risk.

Growth trajectories provide a complementary example of cross-disorder phenomena. Reports of abnormal somatic and brain growth in autism have encouraged interest in whether accelerated or dysregulated growth indexes a broader neurodevelopmental liability rather than an autism-specific marker. Pilot evidence suggests that atypical growth patterns may also be observed in other childhood psychiatric conditions, cautioning against overly specific interpretations of early overgrowth findings ref [7]. Longitudinal imaging studies further indicate that developmental timing and rate of change, more than single early measurements, may better distinguish different pathways to later disorder.

Taken together, these findings argue for models that emphasize shared intermediate phenotypes and divergence over time. Early-emerging cross-disorder features may reflect common perturbations in arousal regulation, attentional control, sensorimotor development, or brain maturation, with later specialization shaped by gene-environment interplay and cascading developmental effects. For infant-risk research, the implication is that both level and slope of change should be modeled, and that transdiagnostic phenotypes may be as informative as early signs presumed to be disorder-specific ref [7], ref [69].

subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Frameworks for Intermediate Phenotypes
subsections.content:
A useful framework for integrating early markers of autism and ADHD is the concept of intermediate phenotypes, often discussed in psychiatry under the related rubric of endophenotypes. In its original formulation, an endophenotype is a measurable trait that lies between genotype and clinical syndrome, is associated with illness, shows heritability and familial aggregation, and is present—at least in attenuated form—in unaffected relatives ref [70], ref [2]. Applied developmentally, this framework encourages investigators to move beyond categorical outcomes and instead track early-emerging dimensions of attention control, motor coordination, sensory response, and language organization that may index liability before disorder-specific symptom patterns are fully consolidated ref [3], ref [4].

For infant research, however, a strict endophenotype model requires modification. Many early traits are probabilistic rather than syndrome-specific, vary substantially with age, and may index broad neurodevelopmental liability rather than a single disorder. This has led to transactional and developmental-cascade accounts in which early perturbations in domain-general systems alter later learning opportunities and thereby shape multiple behavioral outcomes ref [5], ref [6]. Within such models, intermediate phenotypes are best understood as dynamic developmental processes—such as atypical attentional engagement or reduced motor exploration—whose significance depends on timing, context, and interaction with the environment ref [4], ref [7].

This broader conceptualization is especially valuable for interpreting overlap between autism and ADHD. Rather than assuming one-to-one mappings between infant markers and later diagnoses, cross-disorder phenotypes may reflect shared genetic influence, pleiotropic neural mechanisms, or downstream effects of common liabilities on emerging cognition and social communication ref [3], ref [8]. A developmental intermediate-phenotype framework therefore supports dimensional measurement, repeated longitudinal sampling, and family-based designs, all of which are better suited than static case-control contrasts to identifying which early pathways are shared, which are disorder-enriched, and which mark general risk for psychopathology ref [70], ref [2], ref [6].
